title: Alcohol and Gout: Beer, Wine, Liquor and Flare Risk
excerpt: Does alcohol cause gout? How drinking raises uric acid, why beer is the worst choice, whether wine or liquor is safer, drinking on gout medication, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Does alcohol cause gout? How drinking raises uric acid, why beer is worst, whether wine or liquor is safer, and how to drink if you have gout.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, alcohol can trigger gout, and it can make gout more likely to start in the first place. Alcohol raises the level of uric acid in your blood in two ways at once: it makes your body produce more of it, and it makes your kidneys get rid of less of it. Beer is the worst offender because it also contains purines, the raw material your body turns into uric acid. Spirits come next. Wine looked the least risky in older research, but newer work found that any type of alcohol raised the short-term risk of a flare in people who already have gout. If you have gout, the safest amount is little or none, especially during or right after an attack.

**The quick rules:** If you're in the middle of a gout flare, don't drink until it has fully settled. If you have gout and still drink, keep it to small amounts on occasional days rather than several drinks in one sitting, choose wine or a measured spirit over beer, skip sugary mixers, and drink plenty of water. If you take a uric-acid-lowering medicine such as allopurinol, keep taking it as prescribed and ask your doctor how much alcohol, if any, fits your plan.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **See a doctor promptly if** you have a sudden, very painful, hot, red, swollen joint for the first time, because gout needs a proper diagnosis and other conditions can look like it. **Get care the same day or go to urgent care or the emergency room if** a painful swollen joint comes with a fever, chills, or you feel generally unwell, because a joint infection (septic arthritis) can look like gout and needs urgent treatment. Also see your doctor if flares keep coming back, if you notice lumps under the skin near joints, or if you have kidney stones or signs of kidney trouble. If you're on any gout medication, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before changing how much you drink or how you take your medicine.

## What Gout Actually Is, in Plain Words

Gout is a type of arthritis caused by crystals. Your blood always carries some **uric acid**, a waste product your body makes when it breaks down substances called **purines**. Purines come from two places: your own cells, which are constantly being recycled, and food and drink.

Normally your kidneys filter out most uric acid and you pass it in urine. When there's more uric acid than your body can keep dissolved, it can form tiny, needle-shaped crystals of a salt called monosodium urate. These crystals tend to settle in and around joints, especially cooler ones far from the center of the body. That's why the classic first gout attack is in the joint at the base of the big toe, though it can also hit the ankle, foot, knee, wrist, or fingers.

A **gout flare** happens when your immune system notices those crystals and attacks them. The result is sudden, intense inflammation. People often describe it as waking up in the night with a toe that feels broken or on fire, so tender that even a bed sheet touching it hurts. The joint usually turns red or purplish, swollen, and hot. A flare often peaks within a day and settles over one to two weeks, even without treatment, but treatment can shorten it a lot.

High uric acid in the blood is called **hyperuricemia**. Plenty of people have high uric acid and never get gout, but the higher and longer it stays up, the more likely crystals are to form. That's the key link to alcohol: anything that pushes uric acid higher, even temporarily, can tip someone with crystals already in their joints into a flare.

## Does Alcohol Cause Gout?

Alcohol is a well-established risk factor for gout, both for developing it in the first place and for setting off flares in people who already have it. It isn't the only cause. Genetics, kidney function, body weight, high blood pressure, some medicines (such as certain water pills), and diet all play a part, and many people who drink never get gout. But among the things you can change, alcohol is one of the biggest.

### How alcohol raises uric acid

Alcohol pushes uric acid up through several routes at once. Here's what happens in your body when you drink:

1. **Your kidneys excrete less uric acid.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, it produces a lot of a substance called lactate (lactic acid). Your kidneys use the same transport system to handle lactate and uric acid, and when they're busy with lactate, they hold on to more uric acid instead of flushing it out. So uric acid stays in your blood longer.
2. **Your body makes more uric acid.** Processing alcohol uses up a lot of the cell's energy currency, a molecule called ATP. As ATP gets broken down faster, its leftover pieces are purines, and purines get turned into uric acid. In other words, the work of handling alcohol itself generates extra uric acid.
3. **Some drinks add purines directly.** Beer in particular contains a purine called guanosine that the body absorbs easily. That adds to the uric acid load on top of the alcohol effect.
4. **Dehydration concentrates everything.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and if you don't replace that water, uric acid becomes more concentrated in your blood and is more likely to crystallize. Our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains why that happens.

Then there's the company alcohol keeps. Nights out often come with salty, rich food, red meat, shellfish, and sugary mixers, all of which can push uric acid higher too. And a heavy night can mean poor sleep and a cold walk home, which doesn't help a joint that's already on the edge.

### What the research shows

This link has been studied for a long time, and the main findings point the same way.

- **A large study of men followed for 12 years** (the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, published in *The Lancet* in 2004 by Hyon Choi and colleagues) found that the risk of developing gout rose with the amount of alcohol people drank. Beer carried the strongest link, spirits a smaller one, and moderate wine drinking was not clearly linked to higher risk in that study.
- **A study of people who already had gout** (an internet-based case-crossover study by Tuhina Neogi and colleagues, published in the *American Journal of Medicine* in 2014) asked participants about what they drank in the 24 hours before each flare compared with flare-free periods. More drinks in that window meant a higher chance of a flare, and this held for wine, beer, and spirits alike. Even a small number of drinks was associated with some increase in risk.
- **Clinical guidance reflects this.** The American College of Rheumatology's 2020 gout guideline recommends that people with gout limit alcohol, whatever their disease activity.

The practical lesson: for preventing gout from starting, beer looks the riskiest. For preventing flares once you have gout, the type of drink matters less than the amount, and drinking a lot in a short window is the main trigger.

## Beer and Gout: Why Beer Is the Worst Choice

Beer stands out for one simple reason: it hits uric acid from two directions. You get the alcohol effect described above, plus a direct dose of purines from the brewing ingredients. Beer is made from grain and brewer's yeast, and yeast is rich in purines. The guanosine in beer is easily absorbed and turned into uric acid.

That double effect is why, in the large studies, beer had a stronger link to gout than an equal amount of alcohol from spirits. It also explains a few things people notice in real life:

- **Session drinking adds up.** Beer tends to be consumed in larger volumes over a long evening. Five or six pints means a lot of alcohol and a lot of purines.
- **Strong and heavy beers aren't better.** Higher-alcohol craft beers, stouts, and IPAs give you more alcohol per glass, and brewing differences mean purine content varies from beer to beer. There's no reliable way to pick a "safe" beer by style.
- **Light beer is only a little better.** Light beer has less alcohol and fewer calories per can, which helps, but it still contains purines and alcohol. Drinking more cans of it cancels the benefit.

### What about non-alcoholic beer?

Non-alcoholic beer removes most of the alcohol, which takes away the biggest uric-acid effects: the lactate problem and the extra ATP breakdown. That makes it a much better choice than regular beer if you have gout. But it is still brewed from grain and yeast, so it usually still contains some purines. If you love the taste of beer, a non-alcoholic one in moderation is a reasonable swap for many people with gout, but it isn't a free pass to drink it by the six-pack. Our guide on [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol) covers what "non-alcoholic" means on the label.

## Wine and Gout: Is Wine Safer?

Wine has a reputation as the "gout-friendly" drink, and there's a grain of truth in it. Wine contains very little purine compared with beer, and in the large 2004 study of men, moderate wine drinking wasn't clearly tied to developing gout.

But that's not the whole story. In the 2014 study of people who already had gout, wine was linked to a higher short-term risk of flares just like beer and spirits. The alcohol in wine still raises lactate and still slows your kidneys' clearance of uric acid. Red, white, or rosé makes no real difference here, since the alcohol is the active ingredient.

So a fairer way to put it: **wine is probably a less risky choice than beer, but it's not safe in unlimited amounts if you have gout.** One glass with dinner is very different from a bottle over an evening. Sweet dessert wines and sangria with added sugar or fruit juice also bring fructose, which raises uric acid on its own.

## Liquor and Gout: Vodka, Whiskey, Tequila, Gin

Distilled spirits have almost no purines, because distillation leaves the grain and yeast solids behind. That's one reason spirits showed a smaller link to gout than beer in the long-term research. The alcohol effect is still there, though, and spirits make it easy to drink a lot of alcohol quickly. A few strong cocktails can add up to more alcohol than several beers.

Things to watch with spirits:

- **Pour size.** A standard drink of spirits is 1.5 ounces (about 44 ml). Home pours and cocktails are often double that or more. Our [standard drink guide](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) shows how to count.
- **Sugary mixers.** Regular soda, energy drinks, sweet juice, and many premixed cocktails contain fructose or high-fructose corn syrup. Fructose is one of the few sugars that directly raises uric acid, because breaking it down also burns through ATP and produces purine leftovers. A rum and cola has two uric-acid raisers in one glass.
- **Better mixers.** Soda water, diet mixers, fresh lime, or simply water on the side keep the extra sugar out.

There's no particular spirit that is good for gout. Vodka, gin, whiskey, and tequila are all similar on uric acid once you account for the amount of alcohol.

## Best and Worst Alcohol for Gout: A Simple Ranking

If you have gout and choose to drink, here's a rough guide based on how the drinks affect uric acid. Think of it as "less risky" versus "more risky", not as "safe" versus "unsafe".

| Drink | Relative gout risk | Why |
|---|---|---|
| No alcohol (water, sparkling water, unsweetened tea, coffee) | Lowest | No alcohol, no purines, no fructose. Coffee has even been linked to lower gout risk in observational studies. |
| Non-alcoholic beer, in moderation | Low to moderate | Little or no alcohol, but some purines from grain and yeast. |
| A single glass of dry wine | Moderate | Few purines, but the alcohol still raises flare risk if you already have gout. |
| A single measured spirit with soda water or a diet mixer | Moderate | Almost no purines, but the alcohol effect remains. Easy to over-pour. |
| Cocktails with soda, juice, or syrup | Higher | Alcohol plus fructose, often in big pours. |
| Regular or craft beer, several pints | Highest | Alcohol plus purines plus volume. |

Two things matter more than the drink you pick:

1. **The amount.** More drinks in a day means more risk, whatever is in the glass.
2. **The pattern.** A big night out, where you drink a lot over a few hours, is the classic flare trigger. Small amounts spread across separate days are less likely to spike uric acid.

## Can You Drink Alcohol If You Have Gout?

This depends on how active your gout is, whether you're on treatment, and what your doctor advises. There isn't a single safe amount that applies to everyone. Here's how most people with gout approach it.

**During a flare: don't drink.** Alcohol can make an attack worse or drag it out, and it interacts badly with some flare medicines (more on that below). Wait until the joint has fully settled.

**If your gout is not yet under control:** cutting alcohol right down, or out, is one of the most useful changes you can make while you and your doctor work on getting uric acid lower.

**If your gout is well controlled on medicine:** some people with stable gout and uric acid at their target level can drink small amounts occasionally without trouble. Talk to your doctor about what fits. Many people find a pattern like this works:

- Keep it to one or two drinks on any day you drink, not a big session.
- Have several alcohol-free days each week.
- Choose wine or a measured spirit over beer.
- Drink a glass of water with each drink and before bed.
- Eat a proper meal, but go easy on the high-purine foods that tend to come with drinking (red meat, organ meats, shellfish, anchovies and sardines).
- Notice your own triggers. If a certain drink or amount seems to set off flares for you, that's useful information to act on.

### Holidays, weddings, and big nights

Many first flares and repeat flares come after a celebration: a wedding, a holiday dinner, a weekend away. That's not a coincidence. These are the times when people drink more than usual, eat rich food, sleep badly, and drink less water. If you have gout and a big event is coming up, plan ahead: pace yourself, alternate alcohol with water, skip the beer, and keep your regular gout medicine going. If your doctor has given you a plan for what to do at the first sign of a flare, bring it with you.

## Alcohol and Gout Medications: What to Know

Gout is often treated with two kinds of medicine: ones that calm a flare, and ones that lower uric acid over the long term. Alcohol interacts with both kinds in different ways. Always check your specific medicines with your doctor or pharmacist, since they know your health history and the rest of your medication list.

**Uric-acid-lowering medicines (such as allopurinol and febuxostat).** These work by reducing how much uric acid your body makes. Alcohol works against them by raising uric acid, so heavy drinking can make them less effective and make it harder to reach your target level. Both are processed by the liver, and both labels advise caution in people with liver problems. Don't stop or skip doses because you plan to drink. Stopping and starting these medicines can itself make flares more likely.

**NSAIDs for flares (such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and prescription anti-inflammatories).** These are a common first treatment for a gout attack. Alcohol and NSAIDs together raise the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding, and the over-the-counter labels warn people who have 3 or more drinks a day to ask a doctor first. Both can also strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated. Our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) covers this in more detail.

**Colchicine.** Another common flare treatment. Alcohol may worsen its stomach side effects, such as nausea and diarrhea, and heavy drinking can add to the strain on the liver. Ask your doctor or pharmacist about alcohol while you're taking it.

**Steroids (such as prednisone).** Sometimes used for flares when NSAIDs aren't suitable. Combining steroids with alcohol raises the risk of stomach irritation, and both can affect blood sugar.

**Aspirin.** Low-dose aspirin can slightly raise uric acid levels by reducing how much your kidneys excrete, which is why it's generally not used to treat gout pain. If you take daily aspirin for your heart, don't stop it on your own; talk to your doctor. Our guide on [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) covers the stomach-bleeding side of that combination.

## Gout Attack or Hangover? Telling Them Apart

It's easy to blame a sore foot the morning after a big night on "sleeping funny" or a hangover. A few clues point to gout instead:

- **One joint, not everywhere.** A hangover can leave you achy all over. Gout usually hits a single joint, most often the big toe, ankle, or knee.
- **Visible signs.** The gout joint is often red, swollen, shiny, and hot to the touch.
- **Extreme tenderness.** Even light pressure, like a sheet or sock, can be unbearable.
- **Timing.** Flares often start at night or early in the morning and get worse over several hours.

General muscle aches, a headache, and fatigue after drinking are more typical of a hangover. Our guide on [body aches after drinking](/never-hungover/body-aches-after-drinking) covers the more common reasons you might hurt all over. But if you have a single hot, swollen, very painful joint, treat it as a possible gout flare and see a doctor, especially if it's the first time.

## What Helps Besides Cutting Back on Alcohol

Alcohol is just one piece of gout. The biggest long-term tool is getting your uric acid down and keeping it down, which for many people means medicine. Lifestyle changes help alongside that:

- **Stay well hydrated.** Water helps your kidneys clear uric acid. This also helps with [kidney stones](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-kidney-stones), which share some of the same uric-acid chemistry.
- **Limit sugary drinks.** Sodas and sweetened juices with lots of fructose raise uric acid even without alcohol.
- **Go easy on high-purine foods.** Organ meats, red meat, and some seafood (anchovies, sardines, mussels, scallops) are the main ones. You don't need to eliminate them all, but big portions are a common trigger.
- **Low-fat dairy and coffee.** Both have been linked to lower uric acid or lower gout risk in observational studies. That doesn't prove they prevent gout, but they're reasonable choices.
- **Cherries.** A case-crossover study published in *Arthritis & Rheumatism* in 2012 found that eating cherries was associated with fewer gout flares. It's an association, not proof, but cherries are a harmless addition for most people.
- **Weight.** Gradual weight loss tends to lower uric acid. Crash diets and fasting can briefly raise it, so slow and steady is better.

If you have gout, regular checkups with your doctor to measure uric acid are the best way to know whether your plan is working. For a wider look at how drinking affects swelling and inflammation in the body, see our guide to [alcohol and inflammation](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-inflammation-complete-health-impact-guide-2025).

## Does DHM Help With Gout?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that we cover on this site because it's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangovers. It's fair to ask whether it helps with gout. The honest answer: **there is no good evidence that DHM lowers uric acid or prevents gout flares in people.** A handful of lab and animal studies have looked at related questions, but nothing that should change how you manage gout. DHM is not a substitute for gout medicine, and it doesn't cancel out the uric-acid effect of drinking.

If you have gout and are interested in DHM for hangovers, check with your doctor first, especially if you take allopurinol, colchicine, or other prescription medicines. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what is and isn't known. For people who drink and want to try it for next-day symptoms, well-reviewed options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. The most reliable way to protect against both hangovers and gout flares is still the same: drink less, drink slower, and drink plenty of water.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol raises uric acid by making your body produce more of it and your kidneys clear less of it. That's how it triggers gout.
- Beer is the riskiest drink for gout because it adds purines on top of the alcohol. Spirits are less risky, and wine looked least risky for developing gout in older research.
- For people who already have gout, any type of alcohol can raise the short-term risk of a flare, and the amount you drink in a day matters most.
- Don't drink during a flare. If your gout is under control and your doctor agrees, small, occasional amounts with plenty of water are far less risky than a big night out.
- Keep taking uric-acid-lowering medicine as prescribed, and ask your doctor or pharmacist about alcohol with any gout medicine.
- A hot, swollen joint with fever or chills needs same-day medical care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol cause gout?**

Alcohol is a well-established risk factor for gout. It raises uric acid in the blood by increasing how much your body makes and reducing how much your kidneys clear. Over time, high uric acid can form crystals in joints that cause gout flares. Alcohol isn't the only cause, since genetics, kidney function, weight, diet, and some medicines also matter, but it's one of the biggest factors you can change.

**Is beer bad for gout?**

Yes, beer is generally considered the worst alcoholic drink for gout. It raises uric acid through the alcohol itself and also contains purines from grain and brewer's yeast, which the body turns into more uric acid. In a large long-term study of men, beer had the strongest link to developing gout of any drink type.

**What is the best alcohol to drink if you have gout?**

No alcohol is good for gout, but some choices are less risky than others. A single glass of dry wine or a measured spirit with soda water or a diet mixer is generally less risky than beer or sugary cocktails. The amount matters more than the type: one or two drinks on an occasional day is far less likely to trigger a flare than a big night out.

**Can I drink alcohol during a gout flare?**

It's best not to. Alcohol can make a flare worse or last longer, and it can interact with flare treatments such as NSAIDs (stomach bleeding risk) and colchicine (stomach side effects). Wait until the joint has fully settled, and talk to your doctor about what's safe for you.

**Is wine bad for gout?**

Wine contains far fewer purines than beer, and in older research moderate wine drinking wasn't clearly linked to developing gout. But a 2014 study of people who already had gout found that wine, like beer and spirits, was linked to a higher short-term risk of flares. Wine is probably less risky than beer, but it isn't safe in unlimited amounts if you have gout.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking allopurinol?**

There's no dangerous direct reaction between allopurinol and a small amount of alcohol for most people, but alcohol raises uric acid and works against the medicine, so heavy drinking can make it less effective. Keep taking allopurinol as prescribed, don't skip doses because you plan to drink, and ask your doctor how much alcohol, if any, fits your treatment plan.

**Is non-alcoholic beer OK for gout?**

Non-alcoholic beer is a much better choice than regular beer because it removes most of the alcohol, which is the main way drinking raises uric acid. It still contains some purines from grain and yeast, so moderation still matters. Many people with gout find one or two non-alcoholic beers a reasonable swap.

**How long after drinking can a gout attack start?**

Flares linked to drinking often start within a day or so, frequently overnight or early the next morning. In one study of people with gout, the number of drinks in the previous 24 hours was linked to the chance of a flare. If you wake up after a big night with a hot, swollen, very painful joint, it could be gout, and a first episode should be checked by a doctor.
